items.title: Dave Robinson interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007
items.q: the New Orleans revival style which came to prominence in the forties with people like George Lewis and Bunk Johnson

ctx.x: Can you pinpoint what’s the major difference between those traditional jazz styles? Is it in the rhythm section or is it in the horn ensemble playing?

Well both. So for instance we have — there’s various terms and there’s a lot of disagreement of course, of these various styles. But my view, which sort of forms the basis of this traditional jazz curriculum kit that I’ve developed, is that I think most people in the traditional jazz community would agree that there’s at least three sort of main branches of what we call traditional jazz or Dixieland. There’s a New Orleans branch, a Chicago branch and a San Francisco branch. Most people would agree although even…

more loose, kind of a laid back sound, a little more rough and ragged but very much from the heart. It’s almost like a folk music. It tells a story. It’s played right from the heart and it doesn’t concern itself overly with European conventions, the classical European tradition as far as pitch and intonation and so forth. It’s all about how can I tell a story. And then you have the Chicago style, which is more smooth and swingy kind of a feel, more maybe technically accomplished playing, a little bit more…
